project.name: ai-agent-simulator
project.description: An interactive, educational visualizer that X-rays a real agentic AI request lifecycle: you type a message, a real LangGraph agent (RAG -> MCP tools -> LLM) runs and emits every stage as a stream of trace events, and the frontend animates those events across a graph of "stations" you can click to inspect the real data. Nothing is mocked and it runs only against OpenAI; bilingual en/pt, built spec-first and test-first. Note: this project has over 100 source files; consider scoping analysis to a subdirectory for faster results.

tour.title: Two Entry Points
tour.description: The whole app is two containers that meet over HTTP, so the tour starts at both front doors. On the client, main.tsx mounts the React tree and App.tsx wires up the shell (canvas, chat, inspector, settings) that the user actually sees. On the server, main.py builds the FastAPI app, runs the RAG-index bootstrap on startup, and exposes the endpoints the browser calls. Understanding these two roots first gives you the map before we trace a single message across them.

tour.title: The /api/chat Lifecycle
tour.description: Zoom into main.py's request handler, the spine of the project. A chat request loads recent history (db.read), runs the LangGraph agent, streams every stage back to the browser as trace events over SSE, then persists the turn (db.write). Notice the load-bearing idea: the backend never renders anything — it only emits a truthful event stream, and the frontend is a pure projection of that stream. config.py holds the settings (model, API key, DB paths) and fails fast when OPENAI_API_KEY is missing, because there is no mock mode.

tour.title: The Event Protocol Is the Contract
tour.description: Everything downstream depends on one shared vocabulary. schemas.py defines Stage, Phase, and TraceEvent on the Python side; events.ts is its hand-maintained TypeScript mirror on the browser side (the #2 most depended-upon file in the codebase). When you change one you MUST change the other — the two files ARE the contract between backend and frontend. Every animation, inspector panel, and timeline phase is keyed off these enums, which is why they sit at the center of the dependency graph.
tour.languageLesson: The protocol is duplicated by hand across a Python Pydantic model and a TypeScript type on purpose: there is no codegen. A schema-parity discipline (and tests) keeps them in lockstep, trading automation for an explicit, reviewable contract boundary.

tour.title: Emitting the Trace
tour.description: trace.py is how every pipeline stage speaks the protocol from Step 3. A TraceEmitter is threaded through the whole request; `async with emitter.stage(Stage.X) as rec:` emits a START on entry, auto-times the body, and emits an END with the stage's real data and metrics on exit, while `emit()` handles one-shot and per-token PROGRESS events. Each event is both streamed live to the browser and persisted to SQLite in real time, so a trace can be replayed after a restart. This emitter is what makes the pipeline observable.
tour.languageLesson: The async context manager (`async with ... as rec`) is the perfect fit for a timed span: __aenter__ emits START, __aexit__ emits END with elapsed time even if the body raises. This is the same pattern OpenTelemetry spans use, hand-rolled here for the trace protocol.

tour.title: The Agent — A Bounded ReAct Loop
tour.description: graph.py is the heart of the simulation: a LangGraph state machine `START → route → think ⇄ tools → generate → respond → END`. The model reasons over a canonical message thread, decides whether to call tools in `think`, loops back through `tools` while calls are pending (capped at MAX_ITERATIONS=3), then generates the final answer. Crucially there is no standalone retrieve node — retrieval is just another tool the model may elect to call, which makes every RAG lookup an honest, visible agent decision. Nodes receive their dependencies from config, not globals.
tour.languageLesson: LangGraph models the agent as a directed graph of nodes with a conditional edge (`_should_continue`) that loops think→tools until no tool calls remain. Bounding the loop with an iteration cap is what turns an open-ended ReAct agent into a predictable, terminating one.

tour.title: Tools & the DeepAgents Runtime
tour.description: This is what the agent from Step 5 can actually do. tools.py defines the native `search_knowledge_base` tool that wraps the RAG retriever — from the model's perspective retrieval is just another callable, the trick that makes it an agent choice rather than a hardcoded step. deepagents.py provides an alternate, real runtime (planner + sub-agents + a virtual file system) that the user can switch to from the UI. Together they show how one agent loop supports multiple execution styles without forking the pipeline.

tour.title: The LLM Provider Seam
tour.description: Every call to a model funnels through one narrow interface. provider.py defines the LLMProvider abstract base class (a Strategy pattern) with `decide` and `stream_answer`; openai_provider.py is the concrete implementation that talks to OpenAI, folds conversation history into the prompt, and streams tokens back as PROGRESS events. Keeping this seam thin means the agent never imports OpenAI directly — it depends only on the abstraction, which is why provider.py has such high fan-in.

tour.title: RAG — Retrieval as a Pipeline
tour.description: When the agent calls search_knowledge_base (Step 6), this is what runs. ingest.py chunks the markdown corpus and builds a persistent Chroma vector collection; retriever.py embeds the query and does a top-k similarity search, converting distance to a 0..1 score. On the Intermediate rung reranker.py re-scores a wider candidate pool with a local FlashRank cross-encoder, and hybrid.py fuses vector and BM25 results via reciprocal-rank fusion. These are query-time sub-stages of one Vector DB station, not separate nodes — the tour treats them as one subsystem.

tour.title: MCP Tools & the Dual Transport
tour.description: Beyond RAG, the agent's other tools live behind the Model Context Protocol. server.py is a real FastMCP server exposing calculator, current_time, kb_lookup, and load_skill over stdio; client.py's ToolRegistry prefers loading them over that stdio transport but falls back to calling the tool functions in-process when the transport is unavailable — the agent behaves identically either way. The key gotcha: every tool is registered twice (the @mcp.tool decorator AND the local-fallback mirror), so both transports stay in sync.
tour.languageLesson: MCP standardizes how an agent discovers and calls external tools over a transport (here stdio via JSON-RPC). The in-process fallback is a graceful-degradation pattern: the same plain functions back both paths, so a missing subprocess never changes behavior — only the reported transport label.

tour.title: Persistence — The System of Record
tour.description: After the agent answers, main.py's db.write commits the turn here. store.py is the SQLite ConversationStore, the transactional system of record, with seven tables (sessions, agents, messages, documents, message_documents, skills, trace_events). It is deliberately separate from the RAG vector store — embeddings and transactional state are different jobs. All SQLite calls run via asyncio.to_thread so they never block the event loop, and trace events stream in live so a conversation survives a restart. This closes the backend half of the message's journey.

tour.title: Pure Projection — Turning Events Into a View
tour.description: Now cross back to the browser, where the SSE stream from Step 2 arrives. sse.ts is a custom fetch-based SSE client (needed because native EventSource is GET-only and we POST). derive.ts's deriveView turns the event log up to a cursor into everything the canvas draws — station statuses, the active hop, streamed answer, iteration count. The profound consequence: live streaming and step/replay are the exact same code path — replay is just a smaller cursor. useSimulator.ts is the Zustand store holding the event list and cursor that drives both.

tour.title: The Visual Model & Its Geometry
tour.description: stations.ts is the single source of truth for the visual model — tiers, stations, network hops, and the cloud-agnostic overlay — and it derives STAGE_TO_STATION, the map deriveView (Step 11) relies on: every Stage must belong to exactly one station or the projection breaks. layout.ts owns the separate concern of geometry: computeLayout places the three columns and reflows them when a station expands. Content and coordinates are kept apart on purpose, so the same visual model can be laid out differently without touching identity.

tour.title: Rendering & Inspection
tour.description: This is the surface the user touches. ChatPanel.tsx sends the message that starts everything; FlowCanvas.tsx renders the React Flow graph reading positions from the layout (Step 12) and statuses from the derived view (Step 11); StationNode.tsx draws each station with a ⊕ toggle for progressive disclosure; InspectorPanel.tsx shows the real trace data behind whatever station or hop you click. Its render switches are exhaustive over StationId — adding a station means adding a case here too, mirroring the exhaustiveness of the Stage maps.

tour.title: Bilingual Prose & Packaging
tour.description: Two cross-cutting concerns finish the picture. i18n/index.ts is the most depended-upon file in the whole project — every user-facing string resolves through it, and the constitution requires all prose to ship in both English and Portuguese. The Dockerfiles package the two-container stack: the backend image runs FastAPI, while the frontend uses a multi-stage build to compile the Vite bundle and serve it through nginx. Together they show how the educational visualizer you have now traced end-to-end actually ships.
tour.languageLesson: Multi-stage Docker builds use several FROM stages: a Node stage compiles the TypeScript/Vite bundle with dev dependencies, then a minimal nginx stage copies only the static output. The final image ships bytes to serve, not the toolchain that produced them.
